What the official sources say

  • A taxpayer dissatisfied with the valuation or equalization of real property may apply to appeal to the county board of equalization. (Utah Code 59-2-1004(2); source)
  • The county board of equalization must decide each appeal within 60 days after the application is made (the Tax Commission may approve an extension). (Utah Code 59-2-1004(8)(c)-(d); source)
  • Tangible taxable property is assessed and taxed at a uniform and equal rate on the basis of fair market value as valued on January 1 (no separate assessment ratio is stated in this subsection). (Utah Code 59-2-103(2); source)

How does Utah assess residential property for tax?

Utah taxes property on its fair market value as of January 1, and a primary residence gets a 45% reduction in that value. The rule sits in Utah Code 59-2-103, which says all taxable property is valued at a uniform and equal rate unless the law says otherwise.

The State Tax Commission's property tax site puts the same idea in plain terms: taxable value on a qualifying home is 55% of market value. Most Utah residences receive the exemption. A few limits apply.

  • No more than one acre of land per residential unit qualifies.
  • The exemption covers one primary residence per household, with exceptions for homes that are a tenant's primary residence.
  • Property that becomes residential after January 1 can still qualify if it is used as a residence for 183 or more consecutive days that year.
  • Transient use and condominiums in rental pools do not qualify, per the Tax Commission.

Who sets the value and who bills the tax in Utah?

The county assessor values your property, the county auditor mails the valuation notice, and the county treasurer collects the money. Utah runs property tax at the county level for homes, so the office you call depends on the question.

Utah has 29 counties, and the code sorts them into classes that change a few notice rules. A county of the first class, for example, publishes tax sale notices on its website, while smaller classes use newspapers. All of them follow the same statewide calendar, but forms, payment portals and office hours differ. If you own a house in a rural county, check that county's treasurer page for how to pay and for any local deferral process.

When does the Utah valuation notice arrive?

By July 22 each year, the county auditor must send a notice of property valuation and tax changes to every owner on the assessment roll. Utah Code 59-2-919.1 requires the mailing at least 10 days before the county board of equalization meets and before any taxing entity holds its hearing on a proposed rate increase.

The notice must show the assessor's value, the taxable value, last year's tax, the tax at the current rate, and instructions for appealing, including the deadline. Residential notices must also say that owners who are 65 or older, disabled, or in extreme hardship may qualify to defer tax on a primary residence. Owners can elect electronic notice, and the county must fall back to mail if it cannot confirm receipt.

If you are selling, read this notice before listing or signing a contract. The value on it is the starting point for next year's tax bill, and the appeal clock starts when it is mailed.

How do you appeal a Utah property valuation?

Apply to the county board of equalization by the later of September 15 or 45 days after the auditor sends the valuation notice. That deadline is in Utah Code 59-2-1004, and the board generally has 60 days from the application to decide, with a possible extension from the Tax Commission.

If the county board's answer is not acceptable, the next level is the State Tax Commission. Under 59-2-1006, the notice of appeal goes to the county auditor within 30 days after the board's final action. The commission may admit more evidence and adjust the value. It weighs the accuracy and comparability of evidence, including sale prices of comparable property under contract as of the lien date, and offering prices of property that was listed but did not sell.

The commission must decide real property appeals by March 1 of the following year. It also adjusts values when the property deviates by 5% or more, up or down, from comparable properties after an equalization issue is raised.

What are the Utah property tax dates?

Tax notices go out by November 1, taxes are due November 30, and a payment that arrives or is postmarked later is delinquent. The table lists the dates that matter most to an owner who may sell.

DateEventSource
January 1Valuation date for market value, and the date the annual tax lien attaches59-2-103; 59-2-1325
By July 22Valuation notice mailed by the county auditor59-2-919.1
September 15 or 45 days after noticeAppeal deadline to the county board, whichever is later59-2-1004
September 1Common deadline for abatement, senior deferral and exemption claimsTax Commission Pub 36
By November 1County treasurer mails the tax notice59-2-1317
November 30Taxes due, moved to the next business day if it falls on a weekend or holiday59-2-1331
By December 31Notice of delinquency to unpaid owners59-2-1332.5
January 31Last day to pay delinquent tax and penalty before interest runs from January 159-2-1331

What does it cost to pay Utah property tax late?

A delinquent bill carries a penalty of 2.5% of the delinquent amount or $10, whichever is greater. If the delinquent taxes, tax notice charges and the penalty are all paid by the following January 31, the penalty is 1% or $10 instead.

After January 31, interest runs on an annual basis from the January 1 following delinquency. The rate is 6% plus the federal funds target rate on that January 1, but never less than 7% or more than 10%, as written in 59-2-1331. When a delinquency goes past a year, each later year adds its own interest until the taxes are paid or the property is sold at a tax sale.

The treasurer can accept payments of $10 or more toward the current year before the delinquency date. Owners who pay part of a bill may direct how it is split between property tax, assessments, past-due district fees and other charges on the notice.

What are tax notice charges, and why do they matter when selling?

Tax notice charges are extra items the county adds to the property tax bill, and they have the same priority as the tax itself. Utah Code 59-2-1317 lists examples such as liens for unpaid municipal water, unpaid abatement fees, special district fees, irrigation district charges and assessment area payments.

A delinquent tax notice charge can start the tax sale process just as unpaid tax does. The statute also requires a warning on the bill when prior taxes or charges are delinquent on the parcel, and a notice about assessment area charges that paying one bill may not pay off the full amount owed or release the lien.

For a seller, that means the number on the tax bill may not tell the whole story. Ask the treasurer for a payoff figure that includes charges, interest and penalties before closing.

What relief programs exist for Utah homeowners?

Utah offers abatements, deferrals and exemptions through the counties, with income and age tests set in State Tax Commission Publication 36. The figures below come from the September 2026 revision of that publication.

  • Homeowner low-income abatement: up to $1,412 for owner-occupants with 2025 income under $44,221 who meet an age, disability or prior-credit test.
  • Mandatory senior deferral: age 75 or older, income not over $88,442, interest at half the normal rate, reapply each year.
  • Veterans with a disability: up to $535,459 of taxable value on a residence for veterans with at least a 10% service-connected disability.
  • Blind exemption: up to $11,500 of taxable value, no age or income limit.
  • Deadline for most claims: September 1.

A county legislative body can also accept less than the full tax due or defer it when it finds that serves the best interests of the owner, the county and the state, under 59-2-1347. Any deferred amount becomes a recorded lien, bears interest, and is due when the property is sold or otherwise conveyed.

What happens to property tax when a Utah owner sells?

Taxes for the year are a lien from January 1, so any unpaid balance is normally settled at closing. A seller should expect the closing agent to confirm the amount with the county treasurer.

A change in ownership also triggers a residential exemption check. Under 59-2-103.5, after an ownership interest changes the county assessor sends the owner a notice, and the new owner must return a signed residential declaration within 90 days. A second notice gives 30 more days before the exemption is lost for that year. A seller who stops living in the home should also notify the county board of equalization that the residence no longer qualifies, unless they moved to another primary residence that qualifies.

What do property tax problems look like for Utah sellers?

Tax trouble usually shows up as a deferral lien, a delinquent bill nobody opened, or a changed exemption after a transfer. Each has a different fix.

  • Deferral lien: the deferred tax and interest are due at sale, so ask the county for the balance.
  • Delinquent bill: pay by January 31 to keep penalty at 1%, or negotiate a payoff before a tax sale approaches.
  • Lost exemption: file the declaration within the county's deadline or appeal by the September 15 cutoff.
  • Inherited house: the bill may still go to the old owner, so update the mailing address.

If the house also needs repairs or has become a burden, a cash sale as-is can pay these balances from proceeds and close without the owner fixing anything first.

More questions about Utah Property Tax Guide

When are Utah property taxes due?

November 30, or the next business day if that date falls on a weekend or holiday. Notices go out by November 1, and a bill paid or postmarked after the due date is delinquent.

What is the Utah residential property tax exemption?

A 45% reduction in the fair market value of a primary residence, limited to one acre of land per unit and one primary residence per household. The taxable value is 55% of market value.

How long do I have to appeal my Utah property value?

You have until the later of September 15 or 45 days after the county auditor sends your valuation notice. After that, a board decision can be appealed to the State Tax Commission within 30 days.

What is the penalty for paying Utah property tax late?

2.5% of the delinquent amount or $10, whichever is greater. It drops to 1% if everything is paid by January 31. Interest from January 1 applies after that.

Can I defer my Utah property tax?

Some owners can. Utah Publication 36 describes a mandatory senior deferral for owners 75 and older meeting income tests, and counties may grant other deferrals. Deferred tax becomes a lien due when the property is sold.

title: Utah Homestead Exemption: Eligibility, Filing and Selling the Home
content:
Utah Homestead Exemption: Eligibility, Filing and Selling the Home

Cash Home Buyers in Utah
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Utah Homestead Exemption: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Utah Homestead Exemption sale
  • Turn the Utah Homestead Exemption offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Utah House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Residential property is allowed a residential exemption equal to a 45% reduction in fair market value for a calendar year (subject to other provisions). (Utah Code 59-2-103(3); source)
  • The residential exemption is limited to one primary residence per household (with exceptions in 59-2-103(6)(b)). (Utah Code 59-2-103(6)(a); source)
  • Utah Exemptions Act homestead (creditor protection): up to $42,000 in value if the property is the individual's primary personal residence; $5,000 otherwise. (Utah Code 78B-5-503(2)(a); source)
  • For jointly owned primary residences each owner is entitled to an exemption, with a maximum of $84,000 per household. (Utah Code 78B-5-503(2)(b); source)
Selling in Utah?
We buy Utah houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What does the Utah homestead exemption mean?

In Utah the word covers two separate protections: a creditor protection for equity in your home, and a property tax reduction for primary residences. They sit in different parts of the Utah Code and are handled by different offices.

The creditor protection is in the Utah Exemptions Act, Utah Code 78B-5-503 and 78B-5-504, and it is enforced in court. The tax reduction is in Utah Code 59-2-103 and 59-2-103.5, and your county assessor applies it. A homeowner preparing to sell may care about both, and mixing them up leads to wrong assumptions about who to call.

How much of a Utah home is protected from creditors?

A primary personal residence is exempt up to $42,000 in value, and other property up to $5,000. The Justia copy of the statute says those figures are adjusted for inflation each year and does not list the adjusted amounts, so check the current numbers with the state.

ItemAmount
Primary personal residence, one owner$42,000
Other property, one owner$5,000
Jointly owned primary residence, household maximum$84,000
Other property, household maximum$10,000
Land counted with the homeUp to one acre reasonably necessary for its use

The statute defines a primary personal residence as a dwelling or mobile home where you and your household live, plus the surrounding land up to one acre. A household here means people related by blood or marriage who live together as an economic unit.

What debts does the Utah homestead not protect against?

The homestead is not a shield against every claim. Section 78B-5-503 lists the exceptions, and a lender or the county can still reach the house in these cases.

  • Statutory liens for property taxes and assessments.
  • Security interests and judicial liens for the purchase price.
  • Judicial liens for unpaid child support or maintenance.
  • Consensual liens created by a contract, such as a mortgage or trust deed.
  • Calls or assessments on water rights used for the homestead.
  • Property acquired through criminal activity.

In practice the exemption matters most to an owner with unsecured debt, such as a judgment or a credit card balance, who wants to know whether the house can be forced to a sale.

How do you claim the homestead in Utah?

Utah Code 78B-5-504 says you claim it by filing a signed and acknowledged declaration with the recorder of the county where the property sits. You can also serve it on the sheriff or officer running an execution before the time stated in the notice of execution.

The declaration must include the following items:

  • A claim of exemption and, if married, a statement that your spouse has not filed one.
  • A description of the property and an estimated cash value.
  • The amount of homestead you are claiming.
  • The name, age and address of any spouse and dependents.

If you do not file or serve it as required, title passes to the purchaser at the execution sale free of homestead rights. For married owners, a conveyance, security interest or contract to convey homestead property is valid only if both spouses sign, which also matters when you sell.

Can a Utah homestead be sold at an execution sale?

Homestead property cannot be sold at execution unless a bid exceeds the declared exemption amount. A sale is subject to the debtor's right of redemption under Rule 69C of the Utah Rules of Civil Procedure, and if there is a deficiency the property cannot be taken again to cover it.

The statute does not describe in detail how proceeds are divided, so an owner in that situation should get advice from a Utah attorney.

What happens to the money when you sell a Utah homestead?

Sale proceeds up to the exemption amount at the time of sale are exempt from levy, execution or other process for one year after you receive them. A sale also does not stop you from claiming or buying another homestead.

That one year window is useful when you sell and plan to buy elsewhere. Keep the closing statement and deposit records together so you can show where the exempt money came from.

What is the Utah primary residential exemption for property tax?

Utah allows a 45% reduction in the fair market value of residential property for a calendar year, so a qualifying home is taxed on 55% of its value. The exemption applies to one primary residence per household and to no more than one acre of land per residential unit.

The Tax Commission says the home must be a primary domicile occupied for at least 183 consecutive days in a calendar year, by the owner or by a full-time tenant. Vacation and second homes do not qualify. A home that becomes residential after January 1 can qualify as part-year property if it is used as a residence for 183 or more consecutive days that year.

Date or periodWhat it means
90 daysTime to return the primary residence declaration after the county's notice
30 daysTime to file after a second notice, or lose the exemption for that year
September 15Application deadline, and the Tax Commission says late applications cannot be accepted
183 daysConsecutive days of occupancy needed
November 30Property tax due date

Missing the deadline can mean being taxed on 100% of market value for that year.

What should sellers know about the exemption after a sale?

The exemption does not carry over to new owners, who must file their own application. Starting January 1, 2027, the Tax Commission says an ownership change, including a deed, a trust transfer or a name update, requires a TC-473A filing with the county board of equalization.

Under Utah Code 59-2-103.5, an owner who no longer qualifies must tell the county on a form and declare the change on the Utah income tax return. That notice is not required when the owner moves to a new primary residence and qualifies for it.

  • Check your valuation notice, mailed on or before July 22, to see whether the exemption is applied.
  • Tell the county if the home stops being your primary residence.
  • Expect the buyer to file a new application.
  • Pay or prorate the November 30 tax at closing.

What if the house is rented out?

A rental can still qualify if it is a tenant's primary residence. Utah Code 59-2-103 allows the exemption for each residential property that is a tenant's primary residence, and the owner files a declaration under penalty of perjury.

The assessor may ask for a signed lease. If that falls short, the assessor may ask for an insurance policy and then a federal tax return showing rental profit or loss. The county may not contact the tenant directly. The owner's own home has to be a separate primary residence for the one per household rule.

What other Utah property tax relief exists?

Utah has several relief programs beyond the 45% exemption, and counties make the first call on eligibility. The Tax Commission lists these by form number.

  • Homeowner's tax credit: form TC-90H.
  • Renter refund: form TC-90CB.
  • Low-income abatement: form TC-90L.
  • Delinquent tax deferral or settlement: form PT-33, with PT-33A for a lienholder agreement.
  • Active-duty armed forces exemption (PT-22), veteran with a disability exemption (PT-25) and blind persons exemption (PT-31).

The valuation notice must also tell owners who are 65 or older, disabled or facing extreme hardship that they may be able to defer tax on a primary residence. Deferred amounts are a lien, which matters at closing.

How does the homestead exemption affect selling a Utah house for cash?

If the house has tax due, judgment liens or a mortgage behind, the homestead does not stop a sale and does not erase those claims. It protects equity from certain creditors, and the proceeds stay protected for a year.

Cash Home Buyers buys Utah houses as-is, including houses with inherited title, tenants or delinquent tax. If you are weighing a sale, tell us what liens or notices are recorded and we can look at the numbers with your title company.

More questions about Utah Homestead Exemption

How much is the Utah homestead exemption?

$42,000 for a primary personal residence and $5,000 for other property, with a household maximum of $84,000 for a jointly owned primary residence. The statute says the figures are adjusted for inflation each year, so confirm the current amounts.

Do I have to file a homestead declaration in Utah?

Yes, to claim it. Utah Code 78B-5-504 says you file a signed, acknowledged declaration with the county recorder, or serve it on the officer running an execution before the time in the notice of execution. Without it, title can pass to the buyer at an execution sale free of homestead rights.

Does the Utah homestead protect my house from the IRS or the county?

No for property tax liens, and the statute also lists purchase money liens, child support liens and consensual liens as exceptions. The statute does mention that for IRS tax claims a homestead exemption on Utah real property is treated as a property right, so ask a tax professional about a federal lien.

What is the Utah primary residential exemption deadline?

September 15 for applications. The Tax Commission says late applications cannot be accepted, and missing the date can mean being taxed on 100% of market value for that year.

Is the Utah homestead exemption transferable to a buyer?

No. The property tax exemption does not carry over to new owners. A buyer files a new application, and from January 1, 2027, an ownership change requires form TC-473A with the county board of equalization.

Are my sale proceeds protected after I sell my Utah home?

Partly. Proceeds up to the exemption amount at the time of sale are exempt from levy or execution for one year after you receive them, and you may claim or buy another homestead.

title: Utah Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling
content:
Utah Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling

Cash Home Buyers in Utah
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Utah Estate and Inheritance Tax sale
  • Turn the Utah Estate and Inheritance Tax offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Utah House? Get a Cash Offer

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Utah's inheritance (estate 'pick-up') tax was eliminated after December 31, 2004. (Inheritance Tax | Utah State Tax Commission; source)
  • Utah inheritance tax returns do not need to be filed and no Inheritance Tax Waiver is required. (Inheritance Tax | Utah State Tax Commission; source)
Selling in Utah?
We buy Utah houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Does Utah charge an estate or inheritance tax?

No. The Utah State Tax Commission says the state's inheritance tax was repealed, ending after December 31, 2004, and no Utah inheritance tax return needs to be filed.

The Commission also states that Utah does not require an Inheritance Tax Waiver, a document some states ask for before a title can move. For an heir who plans to sell a parent's house, that removes one step. The Tax Commission cites Utah Code Title 59, Chapter 11 for the old tax and keeps its page posted for reference only.

Utah never layered a separate estate tax on top. You will not find a Utah death tax line on the closing statement for an inherited house.

Why did Utah's tax disappear?

Utah's tax was a pick-up tax, which means it only collected the share of federal estate tax that the federal government allowed as a credit for state death taxes.

When that federal credit ended, the Commission explains, the state lost the basis for the tax.

Those states are a short list. Wikipedia names six that levy an inheritance tax on the person who receives property (Iowa, Kentucky, Maryland, Nebraska, New Jersey and Pennsylvania) and a longer list with an estate tax. Utah appears on neither list. If the person who died, or the heir, has ties to one of those states, an estate attorney should check whether another state's tax applies.

When does the federal estate tax matter?

Federal estate tax only reaches estates above a high threshold, set at $13,990,000 for deaths in 2025 and $15,000,000 for deaths in 2026.

Year of deathFederal filing threshold
2025$13,990,000
2026$15,000,000

The IRS says a return is required when the gross estate plus adjusted taxable gifts and the specific gift tax exemption exceeds the threshold for the year of death. Most simple estates, such as those holding mainly cash or publicly traded securities, do not need to file. A surviving spouse can receive the unused exemption through a portability election, but only on a timely filed estate tax return.

The IRS estate tax page has the current thresholds.

What tax do heirs face when they sell an inherited Utah house?

The tax most heirs meet is income tax on any gain above the stepped-up basis, not an estate tax.

Under IRS Publication 523, the basis of an inherited home is generally its fair market value on the date of death, or on the alternate valuation date if the estate chose that. If a Form 706 was filed, the value on that return controls. A house sold shortly after death for close to that value produces little gain. A house held for years afterward, or rented out, can produce more.

  • Get a date-of-death appraisal early, since it fixes your basis.
  • Keep records of repairs and improvements you pay for after inheriting.
  • Report the sale on Form 8949 and Schedule D, and watch for Form 1099-S from the title company.
  • Rental depreciation taken after May 6, 1997 is treated differently, so tell your preparer if the house was a rental.

Our Utah capital gains guide covers the exclusion rules and Utah's flat rate in more detail.

Does an inherited Utah house have to go through probate before it sells?

Usually yes, because a Utah house titled in the deceased person's name needs someone with court authority, called a personal representative, to sign the sale.

The Utah Courts self-help page describes the informal route. You file in the district court of the county where the person lived or owned property, and the case cannot be filed until 120 hours (five days) after death. It must be filed within three years of the death. The court then signs a Statement of Informal Probate and issues Letters Testamentary if there is a will or Letters of Administration if there is not.

StepDetail from Utah Courts
Earliest filing120 hours after death
Latest filingWithin three years of death
Who filesApplicant at least 21 years old
WhereDistrict court in the county of residence or property
What you receiveLetters Testamentary or Letters of Administration

The personal representative's listed duties include collecting and inventorying the estate, paying taxes and mortgages on real property, making repairs where needed, filing estate and income tax returns, and selling property if needed to pay taxes or debts.

Who can be appointed to sign for the estate?

Utah Courts lists a priority order, and the person at the top who is willing and at least 21 years old gets the appointment.

  • A person nominated in the will.
  • The spouse, if the will makes a gift to the spouse.
  • Anyone receiving a gift under the will.
  • The spouse, even without a gift or without a will.
  • Any heir.
  • Any creditor, once 45 days have passed since the death.

A person with equal or higher priority can sign a Renunciation to agree to the applicant's appointment. Publishing a notice to creditors is optional under the court's guide, though one explainer says publication shortens the creditor claim period to about three months, compared with up to one year without it. If you plan to sell the house, ask the attorney or clerk whether the representative needs further court approval before signing a purchase contract, since that depends on the will and the estate.

What if the family disagrees about the house?

A disagreement moves the case from informal to formal probate, which is slower and usually calls for an attorney.

If an interested person will not sign the Waiver of Notice, the court must set a hearing. A written objection also makes the case formal, and after one is filed all parties must attend mediation and exchange initial disclosures. Utah Courts calls formal probate beyond the scope of its self-help guide and recommends finding legal help.

A small estate affidavit does not solve the house problem. One explainer from Utah Law Explained notes that the affidavit route applies to personal property under $100,000, waits 30 days after death, and cannot transfer Utah real property such as a home.

What happens to the property tax break after the owner dies?

The 45 percent primary residential exemption does not carry over to heirs on its own, so the home can be taxed at its full market value until someone applies.

The Tax Commission says a qualifying primary residence is taxed on 55 percent of fair market value, and that the exemption does not transfer automatically to new owners. Starting January 1, 2027, a deed or trust transfer calls for a new Form TC-473A under 2026 SB 238. Applications go to the county Board of Equalization by September 15, and late ones are not accepted.

Heirs who sell quickly may never need this. Heirs who keep a vacant house for a year should ask the county assessor what it requires.

More questions about Utah Estate and Inheritance Tax

Is there a Utah inheritance tax?

No. The Utah State Tax Commission says the state's inheritance tax ended after December 31, 2004, no return is required, and no inheritance tax waiver is needed.

Does Utah have an estate tax?

No. Utah has only the old pick-up tax that was repealed, and the federal estate tax applies to estates above $13,990,000 for 2025 deaths or $15,000,000 for 2026 deaths.

Do heirs pay income tax when they sell an inherited Utah house?

Only on gain above the stepped-up basis, which is generally the fair market value on the date of death. A sale near that value often leaves little or no taxable gain.

How long after a death can I start informal probate in Utah?

You can file 120 hours (five days) after death, and the case must be filed within three years of death. File in the district court of the county where the person lived or owned property.

Can a small estate affidavit transfer a Utah house?

No. The affidavit route applies to personal property under $100,000 and excludes Utah real property, so a house usually needs probate or another title transfer.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Landlord gives written notice, files complaint and summons, serves tenant; tenant has 3 business days to answer or default can be sought. (Utah Courts self-help: Eviction Information for Landlords; source)
  • Order of Eviction requires the tenant to leave within 3 calendar days of receiving it; only a sheriff or constable can enforce it. (Utah Courts self-help: Eviction Information for Landlords; source)
  • If the tenant answers, an occupancy hearing is scheduled within 10 days of request; trial within 60 days if more information is needed. (Utah Courts self-help: Eviction Information for Landlords; source)
  • After a foreclosure sale, tenants may be allowed under federal law to stay until the lease expires or 90 days after sale, whichever is later. (Utah Code 78B-6-901.5; source)

What are the steps in the Utah eviction process?

A Utah eviction runs in this order: a written notice, a court complaint and summons, the tenant's response window, an occupancy hearing or a default, and finally an order of restitution that a sheriff or constable enforces. Only a court order can lawfully remove a tenant.

The Utah Courts self-help pages for landlords say a landlord may not change the locks, shut off utilities or remove a tenant's belongings to force a move. Skipping the court steps can turn a simple nonpayment case into a damages claim against the owner.

For a seller, the useful point is timing. The case has several fixed clocks, and the sections below put them in one place.

Which notice does a Utah landlord serve first?

The notice depends on why the landlord wants possession. Utah Code 78B-6-802 sets the periods, and the Utah Courts site pairs each situation with a numbered form.

SituationNotice periodWhat the tenant can do
Unpaid rent or other amounts due3 business days after service, pay or surrenderPay the amount demanded and keep the lease
Other lease covenant not kept3 calendar days after service, perform or surrenderFix the problem within the notice period
Improper sublet, waste, unlawful business, nuisance or criminal act3 calendar days quit noticeCure where the problem can be cured
Month-to-month (indefinite, periodic rent)Served at least 15 calendar days before the end of the periodLeave by the end of the period
Tenancy at willAt least 5 calendar daysLeave when the notice runs out
Fixed term that has endedNo notice needed under the statuteLeave at the end of the term

Business days leave out weekends and court holidays. Calendar days count every day. A landlord who counts the wrong way can lose a week and have to start over.

The court lists separate forms for each ground, including 1001EV for the three-day pay or vacate notice, 1005EV for a violation the tenant can fix, 1035EV for one the tenant cannot fix, 1050EV for the five-day no-lease notice, and 1015EV or 1015.5EV for nuisance.

How must the eviction notice be delivered?

Under Utah Code 78B-6-805, a notice can be handed to the tenant, sent by registered or certified mail, left with a suitable person at the home, or posted in a conspicuous place on the property if nobody suitable can be found.

The court's landlord page adds that each tenant gets their own copy, and the landlord keeps the original.

  • Hand delivery to the tenant.
  • Registered or certified mail.
  • Leaving it with another adult at the home, or posting it on the door.
  • Keep the date, method and the name of whoever served it.

Can the tenant fix the problem and stay?

Yes. Subsection 2 of 78B-6-802 says that during the notice period the tenant, a subtenant, a mortgagee of the term or another interested person may cure the violation and keep the lease alive.

The same subsection notes that where a violation under the subletting, unlawful business, nuisance or criminal act grounds cannot be cured, the landlord may still give the notice. That is why the court has one form for fixable problems and another for problems that cannot be fixed.

What happens after the notice period ends?

If the tenant has not complied, the landlord files a complaint and summons with the district court and serves them on the tenant. The landlord cannot serve the papers personally.

The court's page lists the filing set: a cover sheet, a summons (1105EV), a complaint (1100EV), a COVID eviction declaration (2200EV) and a disclosure notice (1150EV), with the lease and the notice attached as exhibits. Papers can be filed in person, by email as a PDF, or by mail, which is the slowest.

  • Service must be done by an adult who is not part of the case, a sheriff or constable for a fee, or a process server.
  • Papers must be served within 120 days of filing.
  • The tenant generally has 3 business days after service to answer, counted from the day after service.

What is an occupancy hearing, and when can a landlord get a default?

If the tenant answers, even late, the landlord cannot take a default and must request an occupancy hearing on form 1180EV. The court schedules that hearing within 10 days of the request.

At the hearing the judge decides who may stay while the case goes on and whether it can be decided at once or needs a trial. A judge who sides with the landlord signs an order of restitution. If more information is needed, the court's timeline shows a trial within 60 days.

If the tenant never answers, the landlord first checks military status on the SCRA website. A tenant in the military can get a delay of up to 90 days. Then the landlord files a default certificate and an ex parte motion for an order of restitution.

How long does the tenant have to leave after the order, and who enforces it?

Under Utah Code 78B-6-812 the tenant has three calendar days after service of the order of restitution to vacate. Only a sheriff, deputy, police officer, constable, state investigator or licensed private investigator may serve it, per the court's landlord page.

If the tenant stays, a sheriff or constable acting at the landlord's direction may enter by force using the least destructive means possible. A tenant's request for a hearing about enforcement does not pause the removal unless the tenant posts a bond or certified funds approved by the court and the court orders a stay. When a hearing is requested, the court must set it within 10 calendar days.

StepTime limit
Serve complaint after filingWithin 120 days
Tenant answer period3 business days after service
Occupancy hearingSet within 10 days of request
Military delay if applicableUp to 90 days
Tenant leaves after order3 calendar days after service
Access to essential belongingsWithin 5 business days
Belongings treated as abandonedAfter 15 calendar days

What happens to the tenant's belongings and the unpaid rent?

After an eviction the landlord must give the tenant reasonable access within 5 business days, free of charge, to essentials such as clothing, identification, financial and employment papers and medical items. Other belongings can be stored at reasonable cost and are treated as abandoned if unclaimed after 15 calendar days.

A landlord can also ask for a money judgment. Utah Code 78B-6-811 provides for rent plus three times the damages assessed in listed categories, including unlawful detainer, waste that was pleaded and proven, and amounts due under the contract. The court must award costs and reasonable attorney fees to the winning side.

A motion to increase the judgment must be filed within 180 days of when restitution is enforced or the tenant leaves.

How does the eviction process affect selling a rented house in Utah?

A pending eviction does not have to stop a sale, but it changes what a buyer will pay attention to. The statutes we reviewed describe the landlord and tenant case. They do not say what happens to a filed case when the owner sells, so talk to the court clerk or a Utah attorney before closing.

  • Gather the lease, every notice served and proof of service.
  • Keep the rent ledger and security deposit record together.
  • Note which court dates are set.
  • Remember that showings need 24 hours notice to the tenant unless the rental agreement says otherwise.

Owners who inherited a rental, fell behind on a mortgage or do not want to wait through a hearing calendar sometimes sell as-is with the tenant still in place. Cash Home Buyers can look at a tenant-occupied Utah house and explain what an as-is sale would involve.

What if the rental is being foreclosed on in Utah?

Tenants in a foreclosed rental have extra protection. Utah Code 78B-6-901.5 tells tenants that, under federal law, they may stay until the lease ends or until 90 days after the sale, whichever is later. They must keep paying rent and following the lease.

For a trust deed sale, Utah Code 57-1-25 requires a notice of sale posted at least 20 days before the sale, with the last newspaper publication 10 to 30 days before it. Where the loan financed a residential rental, the notice must also be posted on the unit doors or mailed to the occupants, with a tenant statement in at least 14 point type.

More questions about Utah Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House

How long does an eviction take in Utah?

It depends on whether the tenant answers. The notice period runs 3 business days for unpaid rent, 5 calendar days for a tenancy at will and 15 calendar days for month-to-month. After that, the tenant has 3 business days to answer the complaint, an occupancy hearing is set within 10 days of a request, and the tenant has 3 calendar days to leave after the order. A trial adds more time.

Can a Utah landlord change the locks to evict a tenant?

No. The Utah Courts self-help pages say only a court order allows a lawful eviction, and that changing locks, shutting off utilities or removing a tenant's property is prohibited.

What is the 3-day notice in Utah?

It is the written notice to pay or surrender used for unpaid rent. Under Utah Code 78B-6-802 the tenant has three business days after service to pay what is demanded or give up possession. A tenant who pays in full during that window can keep the lease.

Can a landlord evict a tenant without a court hearing?

A landlord can win without a hearing if the tenant does not answer within the response period, but the landlord still has to file a default certificate and a motion for an order of restitution. If the tenant files an answer at any point, the landlord must request an occupancy hearing instead.

What can a landlord recover from an evicted tenant in Utah?

Unpaid rent, damages and court costs, and in some categories up to three times the actual damages. Utah Code 78B-6-811 provides for treble damages on listed items, and the landlord must prove them.

Can I sell my Utah rental house while the tenant is still there?

Yes, an owner can list or sell a tenant-occupied house, though entry for showings requires at least 24 hours notice unless the rental agreement says otherwise. Before you sign, ask the court clerk or a Utah attorney how a sale affects any pending eviction case. Cash Home Buyers can buy as-is with the tenant in place.

title: Utah Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House
content:
Utah Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House

Cash Home Buyers in Utah
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Utah Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Utah Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House sale
  • Turn the Utah Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Utah House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • The 2025 Utah legislature (HB 106) lowered the individual income tax rate from 4.55% to 4.5%. (2025 TC-40 Instructions (Utah State Tax Commission); source)
Selling in Utah?
We buy Utah houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Does Utah have its own capital gains tax on a house sale?

No. Utah does not run a separate capital gains tax, so any taxable gain from selling a house is simply part of your income and taxed at the state's flat individual income tax rate.

The 2025 TC-40 instructions put that rate at 4.5 percent, down from 4.55 percent after the 2025 Legislature passed HB 106. Line 4 of the Utah return starts from your federal adjusted gross income, which already includes any gain you report on your federal return. So the question for a Utah seller is mostly a federal one: how much of the gain survives the home sale exclusion?

Check the instructions for the year you sell, because the rate is set by the Legislature and can change from one tax year to the next.

How much gain can a Utah homeowner exclude?

A single seller can exclude up to $250,000 of gain on a main home, and married couples filing jointly can exclude up to $500,000.

The IRS requires that you meet two tests during the five years before the sale, each over 24 months, and the two periods do not have to match. For a joint return, either spouse can meet the ownership test but both must meet the use test. You generally cannot claim the exclusion if you took it on another home sale in the prior two years.

RuleFigure from the IRS
Exclusion, singleUp to $250,000
Exclusion, married filing jointlyUp to $500,000
Ownership test24 months within the last 5 years
Use as main home24 months (730 days) within the last 5 years
Look-backNo other home sale excluded in the prior 2 years

A surviving spouse can keep the $500,000 limit when the sale happens within two years of the spouse's death and the other conditions are met. The details are in IRS Publication 523.

How do you work out the gain on a Utah house?

Gain is the sale price minus selling expenses, minus your adjusted basis, which is what you paid plus qualifying improvements.

  • Amount realized: the selling price less selling expenses.
  • Basis: the purchase cost plus improvements that add value, prolong the home's life or adapt it to a new use. Repairs count only as part of a larger improvement project.
  • Closing costs: items such as recording fees, survey fees and owner's title insurance can be added to basis. Mortgage points and loan fees cannot.
  • Inherited homes: basis is generally the fair market value on the date of death, or on the alternate valuation date if the estate chose it.
  • Gifted homes: basis is generally the donor's adjusted basis.

Keep the closing statement from your original purchase and receipts for any addition, new roof or remodel. A finished basement or a new roof can change the taxable number noticeably, and a CPA can tie the figures together before you list.

When does the exclusion fall short?

The exclusion does not cover rental depreciation, periods when the house was not your main home, or a separate business portion of the property.

Publication 523 says depreciation adjustments taken after May 6, 1997 for business or rental use must be recaptured, and you cannot exclude the part of gain equal to them. Gain tied to nonqualified use after 2008, when the property was not your main home, generally cannot be excluded either. Depreciation recapture goes on Form 4797.

A partial exclusion is available if you sold before reaching 24 months for a qualifying reason:

  • A work move at least 50 miles farther from the home.
  • A health-related move.
  • An unforeseeable event such as death, divorce or unemployment.

Homes acquired in a like-kind (section 1031) exchange within the past five years are barred from the exclusion altogether. Two timing notes from the IRS also matter for Utah sellers. Service members and certain Foreign Service or intelligence community members on qualified official extended duty can elect to suspend the five-year test period for up to 10 years. And in an installment sale, the exclusion stays available even if you defer part of the gain.

If you end up with a capital loss on a sale that is reportable, the IRS says you can deduct up to $3,000 a year against other income ($1,500 if married filing separately) and carry the rest forward. Whether a loss on a personal residence qualifies is a question for your tax preparer, since the IRS home sale topic does not address it.

What federal rates apply to the taxable part?

Gain on a house held more than one year is long-term and taxed at 0, 15 or 20 percent federally, with a 25 percent maximum on unrecaptured section 1250 gain from real property.

2025 tax year0% up to15% up to
Single$48,350$533,400
Married filing jointly$96,700$600,050
Head of household$64,750$566,700

Income above the 15 percent ceiling is taxed at 20 percent. A house held one year or less produces short-term gain, taxed as ordinary income. Higher earners can also owe the 3.8 percent net investment income tax, which applies when modified adjusted gross income passes $200,000 for single filers or $250,000 for joint filers. Home sale gain escapes that tax only to the extent it is excluded from regular income tax.

How does it work if you left Utah or live elsewhere?

Nonresidents and part-year residents report the sale on the Utah return with Schedule TC-40B, and Utah taxes income received while you were a resident plus Utah-source income afterward.

A Utah house sold by an out-of-state owner counts as Utah-source income. Nonresidents with Utah-source income must file if they have a federal filing requirement, and they enter the full federal amount on line 4 before the schedule apportions the tax.

Utah also offers a taxpayer tax credit equal to 6 percent of a base amount that phases out as income rises, with the phase-out starting at $18,213 for single filers and $36,426 for joint filers. The capital gain transactions credit listed on the form is described as relating to certain Utah small business stock investments, so it is not a home sale break.

How do you report the sale and when is it due?

Report a home sale on Form 8949 and Schedule D, and do it even when the gain is fully excluded if you received Form 1099-S.

The IRS states that you must report the sale if you got a 1099-S or if you cannot exclude all of the gain. For tax year 2025, the Utah return and payment were due April 15, 2026. An extension of up to six months moves the return to October 15, 2026 but does not extend the time to pay, so interest and penalties can still apply.

If you sell this year, set aside the estimated tax before you spend the proceeds, and ask a CPA or enrolled agent whether quarterly estimates are needed. We can close on your timeline if you need the sale to land in a particular tax year.

More questions about Utah Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House

Is there a Utah capital gains tax rate for real estate?

There is no separate rate. Utah taxes capital gains as ordinary income at its flat individual rate, which the 2025 TC-40 instructions list as 4.5 percent.

Do I owe Utah tax if the gain is under the $250,000 exclusion?

Usually not. Utah starts from federal adjusted gross income, so gain that is fully excluded federally does not raise the Utah taxable amount, though a 1099-S still has to be reported.

Does selling an inherited Utah house trigger capital gains?

Only on gain above the stepped-up basis. The basis is generally the fair market value on the date of death, so a sale soon after can show little or no gain.

What if I rented my Utah house before selling?

Depreciation you took after May 6, 1997 cannot be excluded and is recaptured, and gain tied to periods when the house was not your main home may also be taxable. Ask a tax professional how your rental years affect the figures.

Do I pay Utah tax on a house I sold from another state?

If the house is in Utah, the sale is Utah-source income and a nonresident must file when there is a federal filing requirement. Schedule TC-40B apportions the tax.

title: Utah Tax Sales: Redemption and Selling Before the Sale
content:
Utah Tax Sales: Redemption and Selling Before the Sale

Cash Home Buyers in Utah
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Utah Tax Sales: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Utah Tax Sales sale
  • Turn the Utah Tax Sales offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Utah House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • The county auditor conducts the tax sale in May or June, at the courthouse front door or electronically. (Utah Code 59-2-1351(1); source)
  • Notice of tax sale is mailed to the last known recorded owner, the occupant of improved property, and other interests of record as of the preceding March 15. (Utah Code 59-2-1351(2); source)
  • Sale is public auction to the highest bidder for cash; a bid below total taxes, charges, interest, penalty and costs is not accepted. (Utah Code 59-2-1351(4); source)
  • A tax upon real property is a lien against the property assessed. (Utah Code 59-2-1325(1)(a); source)
Selling in Utah?
We buy Utah houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

How does a Utah tax sale work from start to finish?

A Utah tax sale is a county auction of real property whose taxes have stayed unpaid for four years. The county does not take the house at the first missed payment. It moves through a fixed sequence, and the owner can stop the process at almost any point before the auction by paying what is owed.

StageWhat happensSource
DelinquencyTax unpaid after the November 30 due date, then penalty and interest59-2-1331
Four years passProperty not redeemed by the following March 15 goes on the tax sale listing59-2-1343
NoticeAuditor mails notice to the owner, any occupant and other interests of record59-2-1351
SalePublic auction in May or June, in person or online59-2-1351
DeedCounty auditor issues a tax deed after the governing body accepts the bid59-2-1351.1

What counts as delinquent, and what does waiting cost?

Taxes are delinquent if paid or postmarked after November 30, or the next business day when that date lands on a weekend or holiday. From there the cost grows in two steps, spelled out in Utah Code 59-2-1331.

  • A penalty of 2.5% of the delinquent amount or $10, whichever is greater, or 1% if everything is paid by January 31.
  • Interest from the following January 1 at 6% plus the federal funds target rate, held between 7% and 10%.
  • Added interest for each later year of delinquency, until the account is settled by redemption or sale.

Tax notice charges count too. A delinquent charge such as an unpaid special district fee or assessment can start the same clock as unpaid tax, according to 59-2-1317.

When does a delinquent Utah property actually go on the tax sale list?

The county treasurer lists property for sale if it is still not redeemed by March 15 following four years from the date the tax or charge became delinquent. Utah Code 59-2-1343 then has the treasurer file that tax sale listing with the county auditor.

As an illustration of how that reads, a bill that went delinquent right after the November 30 due date in 2021 would reach the listing step in March 2026 and the auction in May or June of 2026. The same statute says a deferred tax or charge becomes delinquent only if full payment is not made before the five-year deferral period ends.

That long runway is why many owners are surprised. The bill may have been unpaid for years with no one living in the house, while the notices went to an old address.

How can an owner redeem property before the Utah tax sale?

Anyone can redeem on behalf of the record owner at any time before the sale by paying the county treasurer every delinquent tax, tax notice charge, interest amount, penalty and administrative cost. Utah Code 59-2-1346 lets someone other than the owner pay, which helps when a relative or lender steps in.

Before the redemption period ends, the treasurer must accept payments of at least $10 on account, with any final payment allowed in any amount. Payments are applied to the most recent year first, starting with interest and administrative costs, then penalty, then tax. Salt Lake County's tax sale page adds that partial payments do not redeem a property and that redemption within roughly three weeks of the sale must be paid in cash or bank-certified funds.

Redemption leaves ownership unchanged. The deed stays in the current owner's name and the account is cleared.

Can the county reduce or defer what is owed?

Yes, in some cases. Utah Code 59-2-1347 lets a county legislative body accept less than the full amount or defer the tax when it finds that the best human interests and the interests of the state and county are served.

The applicant describes the property, its current value, the delinquent taxes, interest and penalties, and the amount proposed to be paid or deferred. The county cannot grant a deferral without written consent from the holder of any mortgage or trust deed. Deferred tax is recorded as a lien that bears interest and is due when the property is sold or otherwise conveyed. So a deferral can slow a sale down, but the balance still has to be paid at closing.

How is notice of a Utah tax sale given?

The county auditor must send notice by certified and first class mail, or first class mail plus a tracked delivery service, to the last known recorded owner, the occupant of any improved property, and other interests of record as of the preceding March 15. The mailing rules are in Utah Code 59-2-1351.

Public notice depends on the county's class.

  • First class county: notice on the county website at least four weeks before the sale, plus a newspaper ad with the web address.
  • Other classes: a newspaper notice once a week for the four weeks before the sale, or five public postings if the county has no newspaper, plus the state public notice site.

The notice names the last known owner, the parcel number and the legal description. It warns that bids below the total taxes, charges, interest, penalty and costs will not be accepted.

What happens at the auction itself?

The auditor offers the parcels at public auction and sells each to the highest bidder for cash, in May or June. The sale can take place at the front door of the county courthouse or through an electronic process that matches the in-person format, so the public can watch and bid.

Salt Lake County ran its 2026 sale online through Public Surplus on May 27, 2026. Bidders registered about a week ahead and posted a $500 deposit by wire, according to the county page. Other counties run their own formats, so check the county auditor's site for the date and rules.

The governing body may accept the highest bid for the whole parcel, or a bid that pays all taxes and costs for a smaller piece of the parcel. It must reject bids on a thin strip around the perimeter or on a strip that cuts off access to the rest. The county legislative body can also decide that none of the bids is acceptable.

What does the winning bidder get, and what happens to extra money?

The bidder receives a tax deed conveying the property in fee simple, issued by the county auditor and recorded by the county recorder. Utah Code 59-2-1351.1 says the deed recites the total paid, the years of assessment and delinquency, the property description and the buyer's name.

A bidder cannot back out once the sale of a parcel is closed. The county can enforce the bid by judgment, plus interest and attorney fees. Any money above what is needed to cover taxes, charges, penalties, interest and costs is treated as unclaimed property under the state's unclaimed property act. Salt Lake County says its deed is issued within 60 days, after the county council ratifies the sale.

If a tax title later proves invalid, the purchaser holds a lien for the amount paid, up to the taxes, interest and penalties, under 59-2-1352.

Can you sell a Utah house before the tax sale?

Yes. Until the auction, the owner still holds title and can sell, and the delinquent balance is paid out of the sale. The buyer or title company will request a payoff from the county treasurer, and the payoff must cover tax, tax notice charges, interest, penalty and costs.

Timing is the main constraint. Because the sale is held in May or June and redemption must be completed beforehand, an owner who waits until the notice arrives may have limited time. A cash purchase that closes quickly can fit that window, and the owner does not need to repair the house first.

  • Ask the county treasurer for a written payoff amount and its good-through date.
  • Confirm whether any deferral lien or assessment charge is on the bill.
  • Check the county auditor's calendar for the exact sale date.

What do sellers facing a Utah tax sale usually deal with?

Problems at this stage tend to stack up. These are the common ones.

  • Unopened mail, since notices go to the last known address.
  • An estate that has not been probated, so no one has authority to pay or sell.
  • Back taxes plus a mortgage, which both come out of any sale.
  • Little cash for the redemption amount in one payment.

Utah's redemption statute lets installments of at least $10 count toward the balance, but the full amount must be paid before the sale. A buyer cannot erase the debt, only pay it at closing.

More questions about Utah Tax Sales

How long before a Utah tax sale can I still redeem my property?

Up to the sale itself. Utah Code 59-2-1346 allows redemption at any time before the sale, which is held in May or June after four years of delinquency. Pay the full amount to the county treasurer.

How many years of unpaid taxes lead to a Utah tax sale?

Four. A property not redeemed by March 15 following four years from the date the tax or charge became delinquent is placed on the tax sale listing under Utah Code 59-2-1343.

Does a Utah tax sale buyer get clear ownership?

The auditor issues a tax deed conveying the property in fee simple, and the deed is prima facie evidence that the proceedings were regular. If the tax title is later found invalid, the buyer has a lien for the amount paid.

What happens to extra bid money at a Utah tax sale?

Money above the taxes, charges, penalty, interest and costs is treated as unclaimed property under Utah's unclaimed property act, not kept by the county.

Can I sell my house if it is already on the Utah tax sale list?

Yes, as long as the sale has not happened. The unpaid balance is paid from the proceeds at closing, so get a payoff figure from the county treasurer first and check the auction date with the county auditor.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

Selling in Utah?
We buy Utah houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

When does a Utah estate have to go through probate?

A Utah estate needs probate when it includes real property of any value, or when its other assets are worth more than $100,000. That is the rule the Utah Courts self-help pages give, and it is the starting point for anyone who inherited a house.

The house is what usually forces the issue. A bank account or a car can sometimes be collected with a short affidavit, but land and buildings cannot. If the person who died owned a home in their own name, someone will need court authority before the title can move to an heir or a buyer.

  • Real property of any value: probate is required.
  • Other assets above $100,000, not counting land or cars: probate is required.
  • Smaller estates with no real property: a small estate affidavit may be enough.

Can a small estate affidavit transfer a Utah house?

No. The Utah small estate affidavit covers personal property only, and the court's own guidance says it cannot be used to transfer title to land or a house.

Under Utah Code 75-3-1201, a successor can present an affidavit to a bank or other holder 30 days after the death. The affidavit must state that the whole estate, less liens and encumbrances, does not exceed $100,000, that 30 days have passed, that no one has applied to be personal representative, and that the person claiming is entitled to the property. The affidavit is signed before a notary and handed to the third party. It is not filed with the court.

The same section lets the Motor Vehicle Division retitle up to four boats, motor vehicles, trailers or semitrailers on that kind of affidavit. Water company shares are excluded. None of this reaches the deed to a house, so heirs holding a house still need an appointed personal representative or another court-approved route.

Which Utah court handles the probate case?

Probate is filed in a Utah district court, in the county where the person lived at death or, if they did not live in Utah, in any county where they owned property. Utah Code 75-3-201 sets that venue rule, and later proceedings generally stay in the court where the first one was filed.

Utah has 29 counties, and they differ a lot in size. Salt Lake County is the largest by population and Daggett County is the smallest, according to the Wikipedia county list. Filing practice also differs by place. The court's self-help page says papers for a case in Utah County go to the Provo Courthouse, delivered in person or emailed to the filing address the court lists.

For a seller, venue matters because the court that appoints the personal representative is the one that issues the letters a title company will ask to see. If the owner lived in Salt Lake City but the inherited house is in a rural county, the case is normally opened where the owner lived.

Who can be the personal representative in Utah?

Any person aged 21 or older who is not found unsuitable can serve, and Utah ranks who gets first claim on the job. The order in Utah Code 75-3-203 is below.

  1. The person named in a probated will.
  2. A surviving spouse who is also a devisee.
  3. Other devisees.
  4. A surviving spouse who is not a devisee.
  5. Other heirs.
  6. Any creditor, once 45 days have passed since the death.

People with equal or higher priority can sign a renunciation so another family member can take the role. Anyone with priority can also nominate a qualified person. This is the step where family disagreements show up, and one heir who will not sign can turn an informal case into a formal one with a hearing.

How does informal probate work step by step?

Informal probate asks the court to appoint a personal representative without a hearing, and it works best when every interested person agrees. The court's self-help page lists the documents for a case with no objections.

  • Application to be appointed, with the filing fee and the district court probate cover sheet.
  • Waiver of notice signed by interested persons such as heirs, devisees, spouses and creditors.
  • Renunciation forms from anyone with equal or higher priority who is stepping aside.
  • An official death certificate.
  • Acceptance of appointment signed by the applicant.
  • The original will, if there is one.

If the clerk approves, the court signs a Statement of Informal Probate and issues Letters Testamentary when there is a will, or Letters of Administration when there is not. The court suggests getting certified copies, since banks, insurers and title companies each tend to want one. If an interested person will not sign the waiver, a hearing is needed and the case becomes formal.

What are the key probate numbers and deadlines in Utah?

The table below collects the figures that most often affect a family deciding whether to keep or sell an inherited house.

ItemRuleSource
Small estate affidavit limit$100,000 after liens, 30 days after death75-3-1201
Earliest informal filing120 hours (five days) after deathUtah Courts, citing 75-3-307
Latest informal or formal filingThree years after death, with limited exceptions75-3-107
Minimum age of a personal representative2175-3-203
Creditor claim period after published noticeThree months from first publication75-3-801
Outside limit for claims that arose before deathOne year after death75-3-803

What happens if nobody opens probate within three years?

Under Utah Code 75-3-107, an informal probate or formal testacy proceeding generally may not start more than three years after the death. If no will is probated in that time, the presumption of intestacy becomes final.

The court keeps some power after that point. It can still decide what property the decedent owned and can appoint a personal representative, but certain claims, including homestead and family allowances and most creditor claims other than administration expenses, cannot be presented. The court's page tells families past the three-year mark to speak with a probate attorney about determining heirs.

Houses are where this bites. A property that sat untitled after a parent's death, with taxes accruing, can be hard to sell until the paperwork catches up.

How do creditors affect a house being sold from an estate?

Creditors have a limited window to make claims, and the personal representative controls how that window is opened. After appointment, the representative may publish a notice once a week for three weeks in a county newspaper, which tells creditors to present claims within three months of first publication or be barred (75-3-801).

Publishing is optional. The court's self-help page says a representative may skip it but might choose it when the debts are not all known. Without notice, 75-3-803 still bars most claims that arose before death one year after the death. Mortgages and other liens on the property are not wiped out by the nonclaim rules, so a house with a loan still has to be paid off or assumed at sale.

Can the personal representative sell the inherited house?

Yes. A personal representative acting reasonably for the benefit of the interested persons may sell, mortgage or lease any real or personal property of the estate, for cash, credit or part of each (Utah Code 75-3-714(23)).

Those powers begin when the representative is appointed, so a family cannot sign a sale contract in the estate's name before the letters issue. A related section allows acts that benefit the estate before appointment to be treated as if they came after, but a buyer or title company will still want the letters in hand.

The same part of the code lets a representative repair buildings, insure estate assets, pay taxes and assessments, and hire agents or attorneys. In practice that means the estate can keep the heat on, pay the property tax bill and clean out the house while a sale is arranged.

What protection does a buyer get when an heir sells after distribution?

A good-faith buyer who pays value for property distributed by a personal representative takes title free of other estate claimants. Utah Code 75-3-910 protects a purchaser or lender who deals with a distributee holding a deed of distribution, even if the distribution was improper or the representative's authority had already ended.

The buyer does not have to investigate whether the representative acted properly. That protection is part of why heirs often sign a deed of distribution first and sell afterward, or sell directly through the representative while the estate is open.

What do Utah sellers of inherited houses usually run into?

Sellers of inherited houses in Utah most often lose time on paperwork rather than on the sale itself. A few patterns repeat.

  • Heirs live in different states and one will not sign a waiver, which sends the case to a hearing.
  • The house is empty, so utilities, insurance and yard upkeep fall on the estate until closing.
  • The title still shows the person who died, and no representative has been appointed.
  • Property tax bills keep arriving at the old mailing address.
  • The home needs repairs that no heir wants to fund.

A cash buyer can purchase the house as it stands, which spares the estate repairs and showings. The seller side still needs the court steps above: letters first, then a deed from the representative.

More questions about Utah Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property

Is probate required in Utah if the house has a mortgage?

Yes, if the house is in the decedent's name. The court requires probate whenever the estate includes real property of any value, and the mortgage stays attached to the property either way.

How soon after a death can I file for informal probate in Utah?

Five days. The Utah Courts self-help page says an informal case may not be filed until 120 hours have passed since the death, citing Utah Code 75-3-307.

How long do I have to start probate in Utah?

Generally three years from the date of death under Utah Code 75-3-107. After that the court can still decide who owned what, but you should talk to a probate attorney.

Can heirs sell a Utah house without opening probate?

Usually not if the title is still in the decedent's name. The small estate affidavit does not cover real property, so a personal representative generally has to be appointed before a deed can be signed.

Does a Utah personal representative need court approval to sell the house?

Not always. Utah Code 75-3-714 lets a representative sell estate real property, subject to the will and any court order. If the will limits the power or an heir objects in a formal case, the court may need to approve it.
